blocks.heading: Choosing a training method
blocks.text: On-the-job training develops skills while working with guidance from an experienced colleague or supervisor. It can use the actual equipment and avoid travel, but takes the trainer’s time and may pass on poor habits or expose real work to mistakes. Off-the-job training takes place away from normal duties, for example through a course or simulated practice. It can provide specialist teaching and space to learn without disrupting real orders, but costs time and fees and may not match local equipment perfectly. Choose according to the task, safety, existing expertise, cost, time and learning needs. Induction introduces the new worker but does not replace all specialist skill development.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tano Stores has a patient experienced clerk and a safe practice account on its familiar booking system. A new assistant needs routine booking skills. On-the-job guidance using the practice account suits the local routine and available expertise. An external course could offer broader knowledge but adds cost and may teach a different system. Prefer supervised workplace learning here, checking competence before live work; a specialist or hazardous task without a competent trainer would change the choice.
